newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles back on disaster alert in case of new flood.
newsitem.headline: Poles back on disaster alert in case of new flood.

text.p: Steady rain over areas still reeling from two weeks of deadly floods put Poland back on disaster alert on Saturday.
"We must expect there will be a new flood in those same regions where it happened before," spokesman Krzysztof Pomes of Poland's official crisis committee told Reuters late on Friday.
As rain drenched the western third of Poland throughout the day, weather forecasters predicted it would continue into the weekend. The crucial question was: how much and where?

"As for the effects, we will see in the next hours," Pomes said, adding that although the rain was lighter than downpours two weeks ago which unleashed the floods, the soaked ground and swollen rivers were less able to absorb the excess.

The lesser intensity of the rain gave hope that Poland might be spared even a return of the floods that killed 48 people, swamped 4,000 sq km and hit a thousand villages and towns including the cities of Wroclaw and Opole.
But bitter experience meant that this time the government and hundreds of thousands of Poles in the affected areas were taking few chances.
Disaster control officials said people who had been reluctant to accept evacuation before were now more ready to leave their homes, while flood defence preparations were better mobilised.
Citizens of riverside communities in the affected south and southwest resumed building sandbag barriers.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, accused by the opposition for failing to reassure people and mobilise effective action at the start of the deluge, broadcast to the nation on television late on Friday to set out aid measures.
"On the proposal of the government, more than 30 laws have been amended -- all so that aid should reach you quickly and without unnecessary bureaucratic procedures," he said.

Apart from seeing through parliament the new laws, including ones allowing higher government borrowing and giving handouts to devastated households, the government has deployed more than 20,000 troops and set up an emergency communications system to replace one that failed last time.

Parliament also hastily amended the communist-era state of emergency law, removing the most draconian provisions so it could be applied in case of further floods for such reasons as to fight looting or freeze prices to stop profiteering.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said he would sign the amended law but did not intend to declare an emergency unless the disaster resumed in full, PAP news agency reported.

The opposition wants a state of emergency now, while Cimoszewicz says it is unnecessary and would only delay parliamentary elections, due on September 21, because polls cannot be held within three months of a state of emergency.
The elections will pit the ruling ex-communists against a strong alliance built around the Solidarity trade union.
Cimoszewicz has said his administration acted effectively, given that the vast scale of the floods was totally unexpected.
The crisis has shaken Poland's zloty currency, forcing the central bank on Friday to sell dollars to defend it.
Friday's rains also fell on the Czech Republic, also ravaged by the earlier floods, adding to fears in Poland because the destructive Odra river has its source there.

Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati, visiting Prague, said the two countries had been coordinating flood efforts including any water releases by the hard-pressed Czechs of excess water from reservoirs into the Odra.
"We have been in constant working contact... and the Czech authorities tell us when they want to release some water," Rosati told a news conference.
As Poland braced against possible new flooding, pictures on public television from one devastated area drove home the terrible effects of the last.

"In the area of Bystrzyca Klodzka we saw communities which had ceased to exist," a reporter commented, to pictures of shattered homes draped in mud and filth. "Going through it, you believe this area was totally bombarded."
